_schema.description: Combined interaction + condition warnings, referencing ingredients.json by integer id.

fields.ingredient_ids: array of ingredient ids from ingredients.json. Length 2 for 'interaction'. Length 1 for 'condition'.
fields.ingredient_names_ref: display names, for human readability only — not used for matching
fields.condition: string, only for warning_type='condition' (e.g. 'pregnancy', 'rosacea'). null for 'interaction'
fields.is_hard_contraindication: boolean — true is rare, most skincare guidance is best-practice/caution, not absolute

entries.description: Combining can reduce retinol's stability/effectiveness and significantly increase dryness and irritation, since both are already high-irritation actives.
entries.action: Use on alternate nights (e.g. retinol PM one night, benzoyl peroxide the next), or one AM / one PM.
entries.note: Dermatology consensus on combining high-irritation actives

entries.description: Both increase cell turnover and sensitize the skin; combined same-routine use raises the risk of redness, peeling, and barrier disruption.
entries.action: Avoid using in the same routine. Alternate nights or space out by building tolerance gradually.

entries.description: Similar to combining retinol with other exfoliating acids — cumulative irritation risk, especially for drier or sensitive skin.
entries.action: Introduce one at a time; if using both, alternate nights rather than layering together.

entries.description: L-Ascorbic Acid works best at a low pH while retinol is more stable at a more neutral pH; combining can reduce effectiveness of both and increase irritation. This is a formulation/best-practice caution, not a safety hazard.
entries.action: Common practical approach: Vitamin C in the AM routine, retinol in the PM routine.
entries.note: Widely cited formulation chemistry guidance (best-practice, not high-certainty clinical evidence)

entries.description: Topical retinol and other retinoids are generally avoided during pregnancy due to potential vitamin A-related risk to fetal development.
entries.action: Avoid. Consult an OB/GYN or dermatologist before use.
entries.note: AAD; consistent across multiple dermatology and OB sources

entries.description: Low-concentration topical use (under ~2%) is generally considered lower-risk, but higher concentrations or frequent large-area use should be discussed with a doctor.
entries.action: Use with caution; prefer low concentrations; consult a doctor for confirmation.

entries.description: Fragrance is one of the most common triggers of allergic contact dermatitis and irritation in sensitive or reactive skin.
Fragrance is a commonly reported trigger for rosacea flare-ups.
entries.action: Avoid fragranced products; patch test unscented alternatives.
entries.note: Dermatology consensus on rosacea trigger avoidance

entries.description: Both are active ingredients that can increase sensitivity; combined use may raise irritation risk for some users, though azelaic acid is generally well tolerated compared to other actives.
entries.action: Introduce gradually; monitor for irritation before using together nightly.
entries.note: General dermatology consensus on layering actives

entries.description: At higher concentrations, urea can sting or irritate skin that is broken, cracked, or has an impaired barrier.
entries.action: Avoid applying to broken or highly compromised skin; patch test first.

entries.description: Some studies indicate a moderate comedogenic potential in leave-on formulas, which may worsen breakouts for acne-prone or oily skin.
entries.action: Use with caution on acne-prone skin; monitor for new breakouts.

entries.description: Similar to combining retinol with other exfoliating acids — cumulative irritation risk, though lactic acid tends to be gentler than glycolic acid.
entries.action: Introduce gradually; alternate nights if irritation occurs.

entries.description: Denatured alcohol can strip the skin barrier and worsen dryness or reactivity with repeated use.
entries.action: Avoid or limit frequency; prioritize alcohol-free formulas for these skin types.

entries.description: Denatured alcohol can strip the skin barrier and worsen dryness or reactivity with repeated use.
entries.action: Avoid or limit frequency; prioritize alcohol-free formulas for these skin types.

entries.description: Fragrance itself is not established as unsafe during pregnancy, but it is a common irritant and pregnancy can increase skin sensitivity, so reactions may be more likely.
entries.action: Prefer fragrance-free formulas as a general precaution; not a strict contraindication.
entries.note: General dermatology caution; not a specific pregnancy safety finding

entries.description: No specific pregnancy safety data; treated cautiously mainly because it can dry out and irritate skin, which may be more reactive during pregnancy.
entries.action: Use with caution; not a strict contraindication.
entries.note: General dermatology caution; not a specific pregnancy safety finding
